## PLM, the van Leer harmonic-mean slope (`type: plm`) {#sec-ch04-plm}

<!-- PROVENANCE

sources: OUTLINE.md 4.4

### Summary

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
- A piecewise-linear reconstruction whose slope is the harmonic mean of the two one-sided differences.
- Switch: `type: plm`.
- Second order where the field is smooth, first order at an extremum, and total-variation diminishing.
- The slope is set to zero wherever the two one-sided differences have opposite signs.
:::

PLM takes the three cells around a face and fits a line through the middle one. What makes it a *limited*
scheme rather than a plain centred slope is the choice of slope: the harmonic mean of the left and right
differences, which collapses to zero whenever they disagree in sign.

### Derivation

Write the two one-sided differences as $\Delta_L = \phi_i - \phi_{i-1}$ and $\Delta_R = \phi_{i+1} - \phi_i$.
The slope the code uses is

$$
\Delta_m = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{2\,\Delta_L\Delta_R}{\Delta_L + \Delta_R} & \Delta_L\Delta_R > 0,\\[2mm]
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ch04-plm-slope}

and the left face value of cell $i$ is $\phi_i - \tfrac12\Delta_m$. Three properties follow, and `[C5]` checks
all three on twenty thousand random triples.

The slope vanishes at every extremum, because an extremum is exactly the case $\Delta_L\Delta_R \le 0$; the
check measures the face value there against the cell value and finds them bitwise equal. That is what makes the
scheme first order at an extremum and second order elsewhere.

The face value never leaves the interval spanned by the two cells it sits between, which is the
total-variation-diminishing property; the check finds no violation.

On a smooth field the two differences agree and @eq-ch04-plm-slope reduces to their common value, so the face
value is the centred one and the scheme is second order. The check confirms the limit exactly on a linear field.

### Numerical method

The implementation is `dwm` ([`interp_simple.hpp:57-63`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L57-L63)) and reads as @eq-ch04-plm-slope does, with the
sign test written as a product. The file also carries `minmod`, `superbee`, `vanleer` and an MC limiter at
[`interp_simple.hpp:11-33`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L11-L33), none of which the PLM interpolant calls: the harmonic mean is hard-coded.
Those four functions are dead code at this pin.

### Tests

| test | asserts | tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_plm.cpp` | a constant field is reconstructed exactly in all three directions | allclose defaults |
| this chapter's check | `[C5]` the harmonic mean: TVD, zero slope at every extremum, centred in the smooth limit | bitwise and round-off |

: Tests of PLM. {#tbl-ch04-plm-tests}

No test measures the order of PLM. Second order away from extrema is an argument from
@eq-ch04-plm-slope and the check's smooth limit, not a measured ladder.

### Limits

1. **Dead limiters.** Four limiter functions sit beside the interpolant and none is reachable. A reader
   choosing a limiter from the file will not find a switch that selects one.
2. **Uniform-mesh slope.** @eq-ch04-plm-slope assumes equal cell widths; on a stretched grid the harmonic mean
   of the raw differences is not the limited slope of the underlying linear fit.
